Fixed. Two distinct stow 2.4.1 --dotfiles bugs, both rooted in --dotfiles name translation applied to a *directory*:

1. Fold bug (the one reported). Folded ~/.agents -> dot-agents, stow re-appends the translated name when it needs to unfold and looks for the nonexistent dot-agents/.agents.
2. Descend bug (only visible once #1 was cleared). Unfolded, stow descends into dot-agents/skills — a symlink to a directory — and mangles the path again: 'cannot read directory: dev/personal/dotfiles/.agents/dot-agents/skills'.

Either aborts with exit 2 before linking anything, making install.sh a total no-op.

Fix (install.sh + .stow-local-ignore):
- mkdir -p $HOME/.agents before stow, same guard ~/.warp already had — kills #1 by preventing the fold.
- Ignore ^/\.agents/skills$ and have install.sh ln -sfn it after stow — kills #2.

Key finding worth keeping: a *top-level* package entry cannot be ignored at all. ^/\.agents$, ^/\.agents, ^/dot-agents and \.agents were all tested and all still conflicted, while ^/\.codex (same form) works and ^/install\.sh$ works — so ^/-anchored patterns are fine in general, just not for the entry stow is currently placing at level 0. Nested paths like ^/\.agents/skills$ do match, and against the *translated* name (.agents, not dot-agents). That's why the fix skips one child rather than excluding dot-agents wholesale.

Two things worth knowing for later. (1) PrivateAssets="none" on the FluentAssertions.Analyzers PackageReference is required, not decorative: the default (contentfiles;analyzers;build) writes exclude="Build,Analyzers" into the nuspec, handing a phase-2 consumer the dependency with the only asset that matters stripped. Caught by consuming the nupkg for real; it restores clean and emits nothing otherwise. That is why step 3 exists. (2) global_level is left at its default 0, so anything the target repo states for itself outranks these severities — they are a floor, not an override.

Rule design: flags runs of >=2 consecutive expect(<static property path on one root identifier>).{toBe|toEqual|toStrictEqual}(...) statements in a statement list; reports once per run spanning first to last statement. No fixer and no suggestion, deliberately — toBe is reference equality and toEqual is structural, and toEqual-vs-toMatchObject is the author's call; suggestions have no surface with zero editor reach. Deliberately narrow, with each exclusion a near-miss test case: negation, resolves/rejects, non-equality matchers, indexed elements, call-result subjects, optional chains, two-arg vitest expect, repeated paths, overlapping paths, and any intervening statement. 32 RuleTester cases, 23 valid / 9 invalid, all passing. THREE THINGS BEYOND WHAT THIS TICKET STATES.

(1) The preset was missing TWO rules, not one. This ticket says no-reset-all-state-on-prop-change is 'the one the preset does not enable'. The preset enabled 7 of 9; no-adjust-state-on-prop-change was also absent. (The '8' in dotfiles-9b8.15 was not the preset's count either — that was 7.)

(2) F11's review residue is GONE, not merely narrowed. no-adjust-state-on-prop-change is the exact complement of no-derived-state: no-derived-state requires the new state value to derive from a prop, and no-adjust-state-on-prop-change fires precisely when it does not (verified in v1.0.1's dist — it bails via getArgsUpstreamRefs(...).some(isProp)). setSelection(null) on an [items] change, i.e. the store-an-id-and-find shape the mapping called undetectable, is exactly what it catches. F11 is now plain shelf, no '+ review' annotation. It was already counted under shelf, so the totals this ticket predicted still hold: 25 shelf / 1 config / 3 custom / 18 review.

(3) no-reset-all-state-on-prop-change is close to inert as shipped, and is NOT what moves F10. It gates on 'setter refs inside the effect === state refs in the whole component', counting references rather than useState declarations, so any other read or write of the state silences it. React's own worked example (ProfilePage rendering the comment box) does not fire; only a component that never reads the state it resets does. Probed four shapes through the preset to confirm. It is enabled anyway because its message is the only one that names key, but what actually moves F10 review-to-shelf is no-adjust-state-on-prop-change, which fires on every realistic reset shape while pointing at the wrong remedy ('adjust during render' rather than 'pass a key'). F10 is shelf, with that caveat recorded in the preset README, the react.md skill text and the fixture comment. If the map owner wants F10 kept honest, the option is to leave it shelf-with-caveat (taken here) or split it shelf-for-detection / review-for-the-remedy.

Three custom Roslyn analyzers shipped. Commit b6210cc on branch main of tvrmsmith/coding-standards, pushed (dotnet/ tree plus the root README line that still said the Roslyn rules were unwritten; nothing touched in dotfiles or Meridian.IMR).

TVRM0001 combine-assertions-on-same-object, TVRM0002 no-suppression-before-assertion, TVRM0003 no-assertion-escape-cast — the ids the 9b8.9 scaffold reserved, no collision with FAA0001-0004. All three default to warning and none is ever an error. No code fixes shipped: for all three the correct rewrite needs a judgement the analyzer cannot make (which anonymous object, which expected value, which inner DTO), so a fixer would be guessing.

Two scoping decisions carry the precision, and both were derived from the reference's own examples rather than invented:

(1) TVRM0001 groups on the object whose member is asserted — the receiver's own receiver — not on the outermost identifier. response.StatusCode and response.Headers.Location share the identifier 'response' but have different immediate receivers, and dotnet-awesome-assertions.md shows exactly that pair as a CORRECT AssertionScope. Grouping on the outermost identifier would have flagged documented-good code. A receiver containing a method call never opens a group either, since Load().Page and Load().Age are two calls rather than one object. TVRM0001 also covers the collections shape: HaveCount(n) followed by statements indexing the same collection, while a bare HaveCount stays silent because count-only is the documented good form.

(2) TVRM0002 walks the receiver chain only and never enters arguments. That is what exempts Client.BaseAddress! inside a constructed expected value — the precondition the reference exempts by name — while still catching response.Headers.Location!.OriginalString.Should(). The ?. half is caught on ConditionalAccessExpression by walking the continuation's spine for a Should(), so x.Should().Be(y?.Z) is not flagged. A chained assertion (a!.Should().ContainSingle().Which.Should()...) reports once, not once per link.

TVRM0003 flags a cast (or 'as') to object directly feeding .Should(). Generalized from dotnet-atlas.md: matching on the shape — a zero-arg Should extension returning a type whose name ends in 'Assertions' — rather than on the FluentAssertions namespace is what lets it see both sides of the escape, the bespoke assertions type being escaped and the ObjectAssertions being reached. A cast to a real type is left alone; only the reach for ObjectAssertions is the escape hatch. The judgement half (C1, which target to assert on) stays review-only.

Proof — 19 tests in dotnet/tests/Tvrmsmith.Analyzers.Tests, all passing. Every rule has both halves: the violating shape it must flag, plus the compliant rewrite and the near-misses it must stay silent on. Snippets compile against the real FluentAssertions 6.12.2 via ReferenceAssemblies.AddPackages, not a stub, because all three analyzers gate on semantic binding and a stub could make a test pass against a shape that never occurs. Fixtures include an ApiResponse<T> with its own Should() returning an assertions type with no BeEquivalentTo — the Atlas shape TVRM0003 exists for. Expectations are built from the analyzers' real DiagnosticDescriptors via InternalsVisibleTo, so the formatted message is asserted, not just the id.

Two things worth knowing for later. (1) verify-severities.sh was silently verifying a stale package: NuGet caches by id/version in the global packages folder, so the rebuilt 0.1.0 restored as whatever 0.1.0 was first seen back in 9b8.9 — which contained no custom analyzers. THE DESIGN-BREAKING FINDING: 58 of the target's 60 build trees (bead said 59; actual is 60) set TreatWarningsAsErrors=true. Without a fix every injected id would have arrived as a build *error*, breaking builds that were green — the exact thing the constraint forbids. The CPM research repro modelled 3 trees, none of which set it. Fixed in Tvrmsmith.Analyzers.Local.props: WarningsNotAsErrors += TVRM0001-3;FAA0001-4;AD0001;CS8032;CS8034;CS9057. It is an allowlist (csc /warnaserror-:<ids>), not a blanket opt-out, so everything the repo already fails on still fails. verify-severities.sh now proves both halves against a TreatWarningsAsErrors=true consumer: our 5 ids stay warnings and the build succeeds, and CS0219 in the same compilation is still fatal. The last four ids are not ours to emit but exist only because we injected (analyzer threw, assembly would not load, built against a newer compiler); each is a warning, so under TreatWarningsAsErrors any of them would turn a crash in our code into someone else's broken build.

OPEN QUESTION ANSWERED — epic dotfiles-9b8's Not-yet-specified entry "Enforcing the empty waitFor
callback guideline, undecided between a custom rule, a no-restricted-syntax selector, or
review-only text". What was actually built: the NO-RESTRICTED-SYNTAX SELECTOR. No custom rule was
written and none is needed. It is exported as `noEmptyWaitForCallback` from
packages/eslint-config-tvrmsmith/base.js and appended to the base slice's single
`no-restricted-syntax` entry beside A4's `noOptionalChainInExpect` — one entry because the rule is
a CORE rule, so a second config object setting it would replace the first's selectors wholesale.
It sits in base rather than react because `waitFor` is @testing-library/dom vocabulary shared by
every framework binding. Scoped to the test-file globs.

Complete, with a bounded and documented residue. Covers both shapes the removed rule reported —
an empty block body (arrow or function expression) and the literal `waitFor(noop)` — across both
`waitFor` and `waitForElementToBeRemoved`. Gated by 3 fixture cases x fires/stays-quiet, matched

The third option, review-only text, survives ONLY for that renamed-import residue: react-rtl.md
now marks exactly that case [review-only] instead of the whole guideline.
